study.title: Ruth 4 - Redemption, Marriage and lineage of David
study.overview: The chapter concludes the story by showing how Boaz acts publicly to resolve the issue of Elimelech's inheritance and marriage to Ruth. In the space of the gate of the city, before the elders and the people, redemption is treated with transparency and order. The closest relative refuses responsibility because the cost exceeds his interest, and Boaz assumes the right to rescue the goods and take Ruth per woman. The union receives the blessing of the community, and the birth of Obed transforms Noemi's sorrow into hope. The chapter ends with the genealogy that connects Obedde to Jesse and Jesse to David, indicating that Ruth's domestic history is embedded in God's greatest purpose for Israel.

outline.title: The dispute for redemption at the city gate
outline.explanation: Boaz gathers the elders in the place where legal business was settled and presents to his closest relative the opportunity to redeem the land of Elimelech. When Ruth's inclusion enters the negotiation, the other man perceives the risk to his own inheritance and gives up. The old custom of taking and delivering the sandal publicly confirms the transfer of the right.

outline.title: Boaz takes on redemption and receives the blessing of the people
outline.explanation: Before the witnesses, Boaz declares that he buys everything that belonged to the family and also takes Ruth as a woman to preserve the name of the dead one on the inheritance. The people recognize the act and invoke on Ruth and Boaz prosperity similar to that of women striking in Israel's history, showing that the community understands marriage as something linked to the continuity of the people of God.

outline.title: Birth of Obede and Restoration of Naomi
outline.explanation: The Lord grants conception and birth of a son. The women interpret the event as a restoration to Naomi, saying that Ruth is worth more than seven children and will be livelihooded in old age. Naomi receives the boy and the neighbors give him the name of Obedde, closing the bitterness of his days with new family hope.

outline.title: Genealogy of Perez to David
outline.explanation: The final genealogy connects Perez to David through Hezron, Rom, Aminadab, Nahom, Psalmm, Boaz, and Obed. The book ends thus pointing out that God's faithfulness in the lives of these ordinary people is related to the formation of David's real line.

study.context: The chapter shows a legal practice at the city's doorstep, where property affairs and witnesses were publicly treated. The text also mentions the custom of confirming the transaction with the sandal, sign of resignation or transfer of the right. In addition, the narrative emphasizes that the birth of Obed is relevant not only to the family of Naomi, but also to the lineage leading to David.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter highlights God's providence acting by ordinary means: public negotiation, inheritance laws, marriage and birth. Redemption here has a double dimension: the land is rescued and the family is preserved. Boaz appears as someone willing to take real cost to protect the name of the dead and support Ruth, and this makes visible a biblical principle of covenant fidelity and care for the vulnerable. The genealogical ending shows that God leads the particular story of a foreign widow and a righteous man into the greater history of Israel and the house of David. Traditional Christian reading usually sees in this a foreshadowing of the inclusion of the Gentiles and redemption culminating in David and later in the Messiah; this application is interpretative, not a direct statement of the verse.

scholarViews.insight: The final genealogy links Ruth's story to David's family; this is a central reason for the inclusion of the book in the Old Testament.
The marriage of Boaz and Ruth is presented as part of God's greatest purpose, for this union descend David and, in Christian reading, the Son of David.
The city door was the normal place of the court, and the procedure with the elders shows a simple and public way of resolving the legal issue.

questions: What does Boaz's behavior teach about integrity when a commitment costs time, resources and reputation?
Why does the chapter attach so much importance to the presence of witnesses and to the public recognition of the decision?
How does the restoration of Naomy help to read God's providence in situations of loss and waiting?
study.practice: Try to act with transparency in decisions involving others: work, money, family and promises. The chapter encourages to take on responsibilities in a fair way, without exploiting the fragility of others. It also calls to value people who sustain faith with constancy, such as Ruth, and to trust that God can turn a period of emptiness into fruit for future generations. A concrete application is to review family and community commitments in the light of loyalty, justice and care for those in need.
study.uncertainty: The text provided does not include the previous chapter, so some narrative connections need to be inferred only from this chapter. The notes do not explain in detail the exact legal identity of the closest relative, not all aspects of the custom of sandal; therefore, these parts were treated with caution. Messianic and Christological reading is interpretative and should not be confused with an explicit statement of Ruth 4.
